transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC — 38 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Tom (CTO Cyclone), Priya (Lead ML), Jamie (PM)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick agenda — understand current infra, p95 targets, concurrency, and decide hosted vs dedicated POC, ok?
[00:12] Tom: yep that sounds good, we have like 3 main use cases — product recs, chat support (streaming), and personalized email copy. p95 is the big one for chat, we want sub 200ms ideally
[00:30] Priya: to add, our peak concurrency for chat is around 120 concurrent users hitting model streams, typical prompt length ~120 tokens, responses ~80 tokens, we also care about token/sec since billing matters
[00:48] Maya: cool, so p95 <200ms for streaming is tough on hosted if you need region isolation, but we can both look at hosted with reserved capacity and Dedicated; can I ask about your current stack?
[01:05] Jamie: we're on k8s in GCP, have internal GPU infra (VendorX) for experiments but no operational infra for 24/7 inference yet
[01:20] Alex: and timeline? are you looking to go live for a limited pilot in 6-8 weeks?
[01:26] Tom: yea pilot in 6 weeks, production by Q3 if pilot looks good
[01:32] Maya: ok great. Can you confirm SLOs more concretely — is p95 <200ms for streaming or for token generation? sometimes folks mean different things
[01:44] Priya: good point. For chat streaming we want p95 of latency to first token <200ms and steady token throughput at 25 tokens/sec per session, plus overall p95 end-to-end <500ms for typical 80-token responses
[02:06] Maya: got it. So two metrics: first-token p95 and end-to-end p95. Also concurrency 120 streaming sessions at 25 tps = 3k tokens/sec sustained, peak maybe 6k tokens/sec. Does that match your internal estimates?
[02:27] Priya: yeah that's about right, peaks during flash sales could double. We should plan for 12k tokens/sec headroom tho
[02:36] Alex: ok we'll size both hosted reserved pools and Dedicated configs around 12k tokens/sec peak and p95 goals. For hosted we can route to regional endpoints to reduce RTT, for Dedicated you'd colocate in your VPC — Maya, can you explain the Dedicated latency tradeoffs?
[02:54] Maya: sure; Dedicated gives you pinned GPU capacity which avoids noisy neighbors and improves p95 predictability. But you still get network overhead from VPC peering and your app stack. For streaming first-token latency often dominated by kernel startup and KV cache warmup on longer contexts. Our runtime supports continuous batching and KV caching which reduces per-token latency on sustained sessions, but initial token can be higher unless you use warm pools or pre-warmed sessions
[03:28] Tom: pre-warmed sessions — what's the cost tradeoff?
[03:33] Maya: pre-warmed or keep-alive sessions cost CP units — think of it as reserved capacity, we can give you numbers. For example, a single A100-class instance with optimized kernels can handle ~1200 tokens/sec at p95 ~85ms for token generation (non-streaming) with quantized models; but real number depends on sequence length and model size. We'll run your prompts to measure.
[03:58] Priya: we plan to use a 7B-ish open model right now, maybe later 13B. Any difference?
[04:05] Maya: yep larger models increase per-token latency and reduce tokens/sec; 13B could be ~40-60% slower for the same instance but gives quality improvements. We can recommend quantization and batching configs to hit your p95.
[04:20] Jamie: how do we handle degraded capacity? say during a sale we hit 2x expected peak, do you have fallbacks?
[04:28] Alex: yes our smart routing can fallback to smaller cheaper variants or serve degraded quality but maintain latency SLOs, also regional failover. We'll include fallback suggestions in the POC runbook
[04:40] Tom: security is also key — we need SOC2, SAML SSO for the console, and KMS integration for keys, plus audit logs — can you confirm?
[04:51] Alex: yes SOC2, SAML, RBAC, KMS integrations — we'll share security docs (link) after the call
[05:00] Maya: quick note on benchmarks — we typically measure: first-token latency, steady-state tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99, and cost per 1k tokens. For streaming we measure time-to-first-byte and sustained throughput per session
[05:18] Priya: what about batching? streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs?
[05:22] Maya: batching helps throughput but increases tail latency for the first token; continuous batching tries to balance by batching only when it won't violate latency SLOs. For chat streaming you often configure a smaller batch window and disable large aggregation
[05:38] Tom: ok can you walk through a sample run? like if we send 120 concurrent streams with 25 tps each, what happens?
[05:46] Maya: rough flow — incoming requests go to the frontend, we route per-policy to a backend pool; each worker maintains KV cache per session to avoid recomputing context; continuous batching groups tokens across sessions to maximize GPU utilization. In your case, with 3k tokens/sec steady, an optimized pool of 3-4 A100-equivalent GPUs could be enough for 7B quantized depending on batch config; for peaks 12k we'd scale to ~10 GPUs. But concrete numbers will come from running your prompt set on our harness
[06:28] Priya: what's the expected p95 for first token in that config?
[06:33] Maya: with pre-warmed workers and small batch windows we typically see first-token p95 ~120-200ms in Dedicated, hosted reserved in-region can be similar but depends on network path; non-warm cold starts can be 400-800ms
[06:47] Tom: streaming overheads from network chunking — do you support server-sent events or chunked transfer?
[06:54] Alex: yes we support streaming via SSE and websockets and function/tool calling, you can tune chunk size; we'll share docs
[07:02] Jamie: about token/sec benchmarks — do you provide scripts so we can reproduce numbers?
[07:06] Maya: yes, we'll share the benchmark harness (it's a small Go/Python script) that runs your prompts at target concurrency and reports p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec, with bootstrap flags for model variant and quantization. We'll include exact command lines in the repo link
[07:22] Tom: great. Also curious about inference cost per 1k tokens on Dedicated vs hosted — ballpark?
[07:29] Alex: ballpark: hosted pay-as-you-go is higher per-token but less operational overhead; Dedicated reserved capacity reduces unit cost by ~30-50% depending on commit. We'll send a sample calc in the worksheet
[07:41] Priya: any limitations for on-prem/private? we might need private in future for PCI; how different is the perf?
[07:49] Maya: Private deployments can match Dedicated performance if you provide comparable GPUs and networking; main difference is you manage KMS and some networking configuration. We'll run benchmarks in a private POC if you choose that route
[08:03] Tom: ok let's dig into concrete test plan for the POC
[08:07] Alex: propose POC: 1) exchange sample prompts & expected traffic patterns 2) Redwood runs hosted reserved benchmark 3) Redwood runs Dedicated config benchmark (or Private if requested) 4) produce runbook + cost/perf analysis 5) joint review. Target week of 2026-03-09 for step 2/3
[08:27] Priya: timeline works. For samples — we'll include both short chat prompts and multi-turn sessions with context (10-12 turns)
[08:36] Maya: multi-turns are important because KV cache impacts performance significantly; if you maintain long context you'll benefit from per-session KV caching, but first token after a context shift can be heavier
[08:49] Tom: what about model warmup strategies? we want minimal cold starts during live events
[08:55] Maya: strategies: keep a warm pool (idle pre-warmed instances), use synthetic warm prompts similar to production, and keep session affinity for returning users; we can script warmup as part of the POC
[09:12] Jamie: any risk with quantization on your verified models? quality regressions?
[09:17] Maya: minor regressions sometimes; we run evals tied to your prompt set and monitor quality regressions and fallback to FP16 if needed. Redwood Optimize will give quantization recommendations per workload
[09:33] Priya: can you share an example benchmark result? even anonymized would help
[09:37] Maya: sure — example: 7B quantized on A100 equiv: steady tokens/sec ~1.2k per GPU, first-token p95 ~85-120ms; 13B quantized ~700 tps per GPU, first-token p95 ~140-220ms. Those are ballpark and we will run your prompts to confirm
[09:58] Tom: ok that gives us a sense. On the security docs — can you send SOC2 attestation and KMS integration guide?
[10:06] Alex: yes will share links in follow-up email.
[10:09] (brief cross talk)
[10:20] Jamie: question about routing: can we route certain user segments to higher quality models and others to cheaper models automatically?
[10:27] Maya: yes, routing policies support per-customer/per-route model selection and fallbacks. You can tag premium users to hit larger models or use A/B routing for canaries
[10:39] Tom: about metrics — we need token-level cost, per-route latency, and per-model failure rates surfaced in console. Is that supported?
[10:47] Alex: yes Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, latency histograms, per-route dashboards, and trace-level info for errors — retention tiers are configurable
[10:55] Priya: do you expose raw traces and logs for compliance?
[10:59] Alex: audit logs and call traces are available; for private deployments you can ship logs to your SIEM; we'll document retention settings
[11:08] Maya: anything else on architecture?
[11:10] Tom: one more — we use a mixture of short and long prompts, avg seq len 200 tokens when you count context; does that change sizing?
[11:18] Maya: yes longer seq lengths reduce tokens/sec linearly-ish and increase KV memory. We'll include sequence length in the benchmark harness so numbers reflect your 200 token average
[11:28] Priya: okay, for the POC data sharing we'll provide sanitized user IDs, prompt examples, and traffic profile; any special format?
[11:36] Maya: simple CSV or JSON with fields: prompt, context_length, expected_response_length, concurrency_weight — we'll include example template in the repo link
[11:47] Tom: any gotchas with streaming chunk size and front-end adapters? we use a Node-based socket layer
[11:54] Maya: Node is common; chunking depends on your client buffering. We recommend small 64-128 byte chunks and test with our streaming sample client. We'll share sample client code
[12:08] Jamie: last question — if we choose hosted reserved, can we get region isolation for EU users?
[12:15] Alex: yes we can pin regional endpoints and data residency controls — details in the security packet
[12:22] (pause)
[12:30] Alex: recap of next steps: share pricing worksheet, share benchmark harness, Cyclone provides prompt set, schedule POC week of 3/9. Any objections?
[12:42] Priya: none from me
[12:44] Tom: fine
[12:46] Jamie: sounds good
[12:49] Alex: awesome — we'll follow up with links and an invite for the POC kickoff. Thanks everyone
[12:55] End of meeting
